title: Log-and-continue catch blocks
summary: A catch clause that only logs and then continues suppresses the failure from callers; logging is not control flow. AI-generated async glue code frequently records an error and keeps going.

matcher.pattern: try { $$$BODY } catch ($ERR) { logger.warn($ERR); } // small try body, catch body is log-only, no rethrow/return

source.rule: defensive.error-swallowing

tests.label: log and continue fails
log and rethrow passes

notes: Filesystem-existence probes and boundary-heavy catches are downweighted. Prefer rethrow, an explicit result type, or a proven-safe local fallback.

title: Catch replaces failure with default or generic error
summary: A catch that returns a default literal or throws a generic replacement error flattens the original failure and makes downstream diagnosis harder.

matcher.pattern: try { return $X; } catch { return {}; } // also: catch { throw new Error('generic'); }

source.rule: defensive.error-obscuring

tests.label: default-return catch fails
rethrow with context passes

notes: Generic rethrows score lower than silent default-return patterns but are still flagged. Preserve failure meaning: rethrow, wrap with cause, or return a deliberate result type.

title: Empty catch blocks
summary: An empty catch body silently suppresses failures. It should rethrow, return a deliberate typed fallback with a comment, or validate earlier so the exceptional path is intentional.

matcher.pattern: try { $$$BODY } catch { } // empty catch body, no comment, small try block

source.rule: defensive.empty-catch

tests.label: empty catch fails
documented fallback passes

notes: Local documented fallbacks with an explanatory comment are skipped; filesystem probes are downweighted.

title: Promise .catch() default fallbacks
summary: Promise-chain catch handlers that turn rejection into an empty body or a cheap sentinel (null, false, 0, "", [], {}) hide why the async operation failed; common in generated async glue code.

source.rule: defensive.promise-default-fallbacks

tests.label: sentinel fallback fails
propagate rejection passes

notes: Domain-shaped fallbacks like `{ ok: false, reason }` are acceptable. Intentional fallbacks should be explicit, not null/false/empty-object sentinels.

title: Stringified unknown errors
summary: Flattening caught unknown values into generic strings via `error.message` or `String(error)` collapses richer failure objects; stringify only at the final UI or logging boundary.

matcher.pattern: $err instanceof Error ? $err.message : String($err) // assigned to message/error fields or returned

source.rule: defensive.stringified-unknown-errors

tests.label: error flattening fails
structured error passes

notes: Purpose-gate: deriving a display string at the edge of the system is fine; erasing the richer error earlier in the flow is not.

title: Generic status envelopes
summary: Shallow boolean-and-payload wrappers like `{ ok: true, rows }` or `{ success: false, error }` describe transport status instead of domain meaning when they become the default return shape.

matcher.pattern: { success: $bool, error: $x } | { ok: $bool, data: $x } | { ok: $bool, rows: $x } | { success: $bool, message: $x }

source.rule: api.generic-status-envelopes

tests.label: boolean envelope fails
tests.input: return { success: true, message: "Repository created successfully" };

tests.label: domain object passes
tests.input: return { kind: "created", repository };

notes: A small `{ ok, data }` wrapper is sometimes fine; it becomes slop when it is the default shape for every operation. Prefer typed result variants for real success/failure branching.

title: Generic record casts on parsed payloads
summary: Casting unknown structured input to `Record<string, unknown>` (often straight from JSON.parse) turns uncertain external data into a roaming property bag instead of validating it into a domain type.

matcher.pattern: const $bag = $value as Record<string, unknown>; // $bag in {parsed, payload, body, data, result, config}; extra weight from JSON.parse

source.rule: types.generic-record-casts

Are type boundaries explicit? Question gratuitous `any`/`unknown`/optional/casts and silent fallbacks that paper over an unclear invariant — making the boundary explicit often makes the surrounding control flow simpler.

tests.label: generic record cast fails
tests.input: const parsed = JSON.parse(raw) as Record<string, unknown>;

tests.label: schema-validated parse passes
tests.input:
const input: unknown = JSON.parse(raw);
const parsed = UserConfigSchema.parse(input);

notes: Treat input as unknown until proven: parse into a real domain type with a schema/decoder, or narrow with a type guard at the boundary.

title: Type-check suppression (`as any`, `unknown as T`, `@ts-ignore`)
summary: Escaping the type system with `as any`, `as unknown as T`, `@ts-ignore` or `@ts-nocheck` suppresses the checker instead of modelling the data; slop-scan's type-escape family treats unvalidated generic casts as a strong tell.

source.rule: types.generic-record-casts (type-escape family)
id: 'no-double-assertion' — description: 'Chained type assertions like `as unknown as T` bypass TypeScript safety. AI chains these to silence type errors it does not understand.'

tests.label: ts-ignore suppression fails
tests.input:
// @ts-ignore -- trust me
const user = payload as any;

tests.label: typed guard passes
tests.input: const user: User = parseUser(payload);

notes: Canonicalization: slop-scan ships the `as Record<string, unknown>` detector (ZS-CODE-007); the textual `as any`/`@ts-ignore` variants are the same type-escape tell. `@ts-expect-error` with a real comment may be acceptable in migrations — allowlist the repo's documented cases.

title: Placeholder comments gesturing at future work
summary: Filler comments like 'add more validation if needed' or 'handle more cases here later' vaguely promise completeness instead of explaining current behavior or naming exact missing work.

matcher.pattern: add more validation|handle more cases|extend this logic|customize this behavior|implement [\w ]+ here|add more [\w ]+ if needed

source.rule: comments.placeholder-comments

tests.label: vague future gesture fails
concrete TODO passes

notes: Conservative on purpose: routine TODOs and descriptive maintenance notes should not create noise. Replace placeholders with a concrete TODO that names the missing case, or delete the comment.

title: Pass-through wrappers
summary: Trivial functions whose body is a direct forward to another call add indirection without behavior; a wrapper should earn its existence with validation, normalization, retries, or a stable compatibility layer.

matcher.pattern: export function $NAME($$$ARGS) { return $OTHER($$$ARGS); } // body is a single direct call; no alias/backward-compat comment

source.rule: structure.pass-through-wrappers
Delete a pass-through wrapper that adds indirection without clarifying the API.

tests.label: rename-only wrapper fails
compat alias passes

notes: Boundary wrappers around fetch/axios/prisma/redis-style APIs are exempt; alias and backward-compatibility comments are exempt.

title: Async ceremony (redundant await / async pass-through)
summary: `return await foo()` around a direct call and trivial async wrappers with no internal await make the call graph larger without making behavior clearer.

matcher.pattern: async function $NAME($$$ARGS) { return await $OTHER($$$ARGS); } // redundant await or async passthrough with no internal await

source.rule: defensive.async-noise
SIMPLIFY: Unnecessary async wrapper — async function getUser(id: string): Promise<User> { return await userService.findById(id); }

tests.label: redundant return await fails
real async work passes

notes: Remove async entirely when just forwarding a promise; remove redundant await when immediately returning the awaited value. Edge-facing wrappers (fetch, axios, prisma, redis) are exempt.

title: Duplicate function signatures across source files
summary: Near-identical helper bodies copy-pasted across 3+ files (normalizing local names) fork future fixes; extraction into one reusable helper prevents silent copy-paste drift.

source.rule: structure.duplicate-function-signatures

tests.label: same helper shape in 3 files fails
shared helper passes

notes: Clusters count only at 3+ files; tiny functions and pass-through wrappers are excluded; duplication is acceptable when domain concepts are truly diverging.

title: Duplicate test mock/setup shapes
summary: The same mock wiring repeated across 3+ test files bloats every suite; shared scenario builders keep test intent focused on what changes per case.

source.rule: tests.duplicate-mock-setup

tests.label: same mock setup in 3 test files fails
tests.input:
// users.test.ts / teams.test.ts / accounts.test.ts each repeat:
vi.mocked(api.fetchUser).mockResolvedValue({ id: 1, name: "Ada" });

tests.label: shared mock helper passes

notes: Generic declarations (vi.mock, vi.spyOn) and cleanup-only statements (mockReset, mockClear) do not contribute.

title: Over-fragmented directories of tiny files
summary: Directories with 6+ files where 60%+ are <=25 lines and heavy on wrappers/barrels look modular on disk while forcing readers to jump between many tiny files to understand one behavior.

source.rule: structure.over-fragmentation

tests.label: wrapper-heavy directory fails
tests.input: src/payments/ = index.ts, create-payment.ts, update-payment.ts, delete-payment.ts, get-payment.ts, payment-types.ts (6+ files, mostly <=25-line wrappers/barrels)

tests.label: cohesive modules pass
tests.input: src/payments/ = service.ts, types.ts, gateways/ (small but substantial implementation files)

notes: Asset buckets (icons/, assets/) and test-heavy directories are suppressed; the goal is module boundaries that follow behavior, not fewer files at all costs.

title: Pure re-export barrel files
summary: Files whose every top-level statement is a re-export (2+) add another place to chase symbols through; barrels should improve discoverability without hiding module boundaries.

source.rule: structure.barrel-density
Barrel files are entry points that re-export multiple modules (e.g. `index.js` that does `export * from './module'`). Import directly from source files instead of barrel files.

tests.label: pure barrel fails
module with one re-export passes

notes: Keep barrels small and intentional; avoid barrel-to-barrel indirection layers.

title: Directory fan-out hotspots
summary: Directories whose file count is unusually large relative to siblings (ceil(median*2.25), or repo average*2.5, min 6 files) become dumping grounds for loosely related one-file-per-concept fragments.

source.rule: structure.directory-fanout-hotspot

tests.label: 16-file dir next to 3-4 file siblings fails
tests.input: src/api (3 files), src/auth (4 files), src/billing (3 files), src/generated-actions (16 files: action-01.ts .. action-16.ts)

tests.label: asset bucket passes
tests.input: src/icons/ with add.tsx, remove.tsx, search.tsx, ... (asset-like directory, expected wide shape)

notes: Asset-like and test-matrix directories are suppressed; prefer deeper subdomain boundaries or merging ultra-thin files once a folder becomes a grab bag.

title: Reimplementing an existing helper
summary: A new private function whose body duplicates something the repo already owns (utils/helpers/sibling module) forks every future fix; agents write from the prompt outward, not the repo inward.

source.rule: Pattern 1: Reimplementing an existing helper
Pattern 1: Reimplementing an existing helper (the signature AI tell) — 'agents write code from the prompt outward, not from the repo inward. Every duplicate forks future fixes.'

tests.label: re-implemented validator fails
reused helper passes

notes: Build a mental index of the repo's existing helpers before scanning or implementing (grep utils/helpers/common/validators). Severity 1 if the duplication is measured (hot path with benchmark, vendored code).

title: `_v2` / `_new` / `_impl` clone functions
summary: Keeping `foo` and `foo_v2` both alive with copy-pasted bodies creates two sources of truth; the agent should merge (a parameter or the newer body) and keep one name.

source.rule: Pattern 2: _v2 / _new / _impl clones
Pattern 2: `_v2` / `_new` / `_impl` clones — 'the agent didn't dare modify the original, so now there are two sources of truth.'

tests.label: foo_v2 alongside foo fails
tests.input:
def save_user(data): ...
def save_user_v2(data): ...  # same body with one branch changed

tests.label: documented migration passes
tests.input:
# migrating to v2 API, old path removed in 3.0
def save_user(data): ...

notes: Check git history / CHANGELOG before merging: `_v2` during a documented migration is exempt.

title: Reinventing the standard library / installed deps
summary: Hand-rolled groupby, deep-copy-via-JSON, manual URL parsing, or bespoke date math duplicate behavior that stdlib or an already-installed dependency already provides correctly.

source.rule: Pattern 3: Reinventing the standard library / installed deps

tests.label: hand-rolled deep copy fails
tests.input:
def deep_copy(obj):
    return json.loads(json.dumps(obj))

tests.label: stdlib copy passes
tests.input:
import copy
copied = copy.deepcopy(obj)

notes: Verify the equivalent exists in stdlib or an installed dependency before flagging.

title: Single-implementation abstractions
summary: An ABC/interface/Protocol, registry, or factory with exactly one concrete class or registration adds flexibility for a future that was never requested; inline it until a second implementation arrives.

source.rule: Pattern 4: Single-implementation abstraction

tests.label: one-backend registry fails
tests.input:
class AbstractReportBackend(ABC): ...
class TextReportBackend(AbstractReportBackend): ...
_BACKENDS = {"text": TextReportBackend}  # only one registration, one call site

tests.label: plain function passes
tests.input: _BACKENDS = {"text": lambda rows: "\n".join(map(str, rows))}

notes: Registries/ABCs in actual plugin systems are exempt when entry points load implementations dynamically. Purpose-gate: the abstraction can return when the second implementation arrives.

title: Dead 'for future use' code
summary: Helpers with no call site, parameters no caller passes, and 'provided for extensibility' exports cost review, grep hits, and false confidence; delete them — git remembers.

source.rule: Pattern 5: Dead 'for future use' code
Don't preserve speculative abstractions. If it's not used now, it's complexity without value. Remove it and re-add when needed.
id: 'no-unused-protocol' — description: 'Protocol class defined but never referenced in the file. AI scaffold from a previous iteration that the model abandoned.'

tests.label: unused export fails
tests.input: def export_*_to_dict(...): ...  # 'provided for extensibility', zero call sites in repo, scripts, or templates

tests.label: referenced helper passes
tests.input: def render_report(rows): ...  # called from main.py and report CLI

notes: Grep the whole repo — including scripts and templates — before deleting; docstrings promising 'flexible, extensible, seamlessly' are signals.

title: Config/API sprawl for a local case
summary: A new global flag, config field, CLI arg, or public parameter consulted from exactly one place multiplies the state space forever; make it local or a parameter of the one function that cares.

source.rule: Pattern 7: Config/API sprawl for a local case

tests.label: one-consumer global knob fails
tests.input: settings.enable_custom_mapping = True  # read by exactly one function, no other callers or docs

tests.label: local parameter passes
tests.input:
def transform(rows, mapping):
    ...  # mapping is a parameter of the function that cares

notes: Applies to module-level constants that only one function reads; keep local needs local.

title: Broad exception swallowing (`except Exception: pass`)
summary: A broad/bare except that returns a default, logs nothing, or passes converts crashes (visible, debuggable) into silent corruption; narrow to the exceptions that can actually occur, or let it raise.

source.rule: Pattern 8: Broad exception swallowing
Pattern 8: Broad exception swallowing — 'converts crashes (visible, debuggable) into corruption (invisible).'

tests.label: bare except pass fails
narrow logged except passes

notes: Defensive code at trust boundaries (parsing user input, network payloads) may legitimately catch broadly but must still log, not pass. Error swallowing that logs and is commented is a deliberate resilience decision.

title: Unjustified try-import fallbacks
summary: `try: import fast_x except ImportError: import x` with no benchmark, no extras entry, and no test of the fallback path leaves two code paths where one is untested.

matcher.pattern: try: import $fast except ImportError: import $slow // optional-dependency dance with no extras metadata / benchmark / fallback test

source.rule: Pattern 9: Unjustified try-import fallback

tests.label: unbenchmarked fallback fails
packaged extras passes

notes: The tell is unjustified, not fallback: documented platform differences, packaged extras, and version gates during a migration are fine. If the dependency matters, declare it; if not, drop it.

title: Attribute-probing chains
summary: `hasattr`/`getattr`/`isinstance` ladders that accept 'dict or object or maybe None', copy-pasted at every field access, compensate for not knowing the real type instead of writing to it.

matcher.pattern: hasattr($x, "$field") and getattr($x, "$field", None) and isinstance(getattr($x, "$field"), $T) // probing ladder repeated per field

source.rule: Pattern 10: Attribute-probing chains

tests.label: dict-or-object ladder fails
typed access passes
tests.input:
def title_of(item: Article) -> str:
    return item.title

notes: Probing is legitimate exactly where data is untrusted (plugin-supplied objects) but should not be copy-pasted per field; find the real type and write to it.

title: Paranoid re-validation
summary: Re-checking invariants the type system or an upstream gate already guarantees (e.g. `if x is not None` on a value just constructed) signals the agent never traced the actual contract.

matcher.pattern: if $x is not None: ... // where $x was just constructed/assigned non-null in the same scope

source.rule: Pattern 11: Paranoid re-validation

tests.label: redundant None check fails
boundary validation passes

notes: Re-validation is correct at real trust boundaries, not wherever the type was left unexamined.

title: Narrating comments
summary: A comment that restates the next line, addresses the reviewer ('This change ensures correctness'), or resolves its own TODO in the same PR adds noise; a comment earns its line only by stating what the code cannot say.

matcher.pattern: # (This change|This commit|This code|We now|we now) (ensures|guarantees|handles|fixes)|# Join the rows with newlines|# [Ll]oop through (each|all)

source.rule: Pattern 12: Narrating comments
Comments explaining "what" | `// increment counter` above `count++` | Delete the comment — the code is clear enough
id: 'no-obvious-comments' — description: 'Comments that restate what the code does are noise. AI generates these constantly.'
id: 'no-narrator-comments' — description: 'AI writes "This function handles..." style comments that narrate instead of explain.'

id: 'excessive_boilerplate_comment' — pattern: /\/\/\s*This (?:function|component|hook|variable|method).* (?:does|is|handles?|returns?|takes?|processes?)/gi — message: "Boilerplate comment that restates the obvious — adds zero insight"

tests.label: restating comment fails
tests.input:
# Join the rows with newlines
return "\n".join(map(str, rows))

tests.label: constraint comment passes
tests.input:
# Keep in sync with the upstream API contract.
return normalizeName(input.trim())

notes: The regex catches reviewer-addressed and template phrasing; pure restatement of the adjacent statement needs AST/semantic judgment. One narrating comment is nothing — a cluster with other slop is a confession.

title: Boilerplate / empty documentation
summary: Docstrings that restate the function name ('def get_user(): """Get the user."""') or pad with marketing adjectives (robust, comprehensive, seamless) document nothing the code cannot say.

source.rule: Pattern 13: Boilerplate docstrings

tests.label: name-restating docstring fails
contract docstring passes

notes: Name-restatement requires context (AST); marketing-adjective detection is textual. Docs should record constraints and non-obvious behavior, not the function name.

title: Dead imports, unused variables, decorative banners
summary: Imports left from deleted attempts, `# ===== SECTION =====` banners, leftover print/debug logging, and emoji in identifiers are implementation debris that a healthy codebase does not carry.

source.rule: Pattern 14: Dead imports, unused variables, decorative banners
id: 'no-section-dividers' — description: 'AI generates ASCII section dividers like "// ========" that clutter code.'
id: 'production_console_log' — message: "Found console logging in production code. Remove before deployment."

tests.label: banner and debug print fail
tests.input:
# ====== SECTION: AUTH ======
print("debug: loading auth")
import auth

tests.label: clean module passes
tests.input:
import auth

def login(): ...

notes: Unused-import and unused-variable detection needs AST/language tooling; the regex covers banners and leftover debug statements. Remove emoji from identifiers and log lines.

title: Tests that assert the mock
summary: A test where every collaborator is mocked and the assertion only checks the mock was called can never fail for a real reason; it verifies scaffolding, not behavior.

source.rule: Pattern 15: Tests that assert the mock (report-only by default)
The mock earns no assertions. A mock assertion passes when the mock is present and fails when it is absent — it says nothing about the component.

tests.label: mock-call assertion fails
tests.input:
def test_send():
    mailer = Mock()
    send(mailer, "hi")
    mailer.send.assert_called_once_with("hi")  # asserts the mock, not any real behavior

tests.label: behavior assertion passes

notes: Report-only by default in code-humanizer; fix only with maintainer approval. Test slop inflates coverage without protecting behavior.

title: Trivial or duplicated assertions
summary: Asserting literals, or re-testing the same case under three names to inflate coverage, adds maintenance cost without testing new behavior.

source.rule: Pattern 16: Trivial or duplicated assertions

tests.label: duplicate coverage padding fails
tests.input:
def test_add_1(): assert add(1, 1) == 2
def test_add_2(): assert add(1, 1) == 2
def test_add_3(): assert add(1, 1) == 2

tests.label: distinct cases pass
tests.input:
def test_add_identity(): assert add(0, 5) == 5
def test_add_negative(): assert add(-1, 1) == 0
def test_add_overflow(): assert add(2**31, 1) == 2**31 + 1

notes: Same case under multiple names to hit coverage targets is padding; vary inputs, boundaries, and failure cases instead.

title: Added-comment cap per change
summary: PRs that add more than 10 comments across changed files are flagged: dense commenting is a common AI-slop signal, and comments should earn their lines.

source.rule: max-added-comments (default 10)

tests.label: 12 added comments fails
tests.input: PR diff adds 12 comment lines across 3 changed files

tests.label: 5 added comments passes
tests.input: PR diff adds 5 comment lines across 3 changed files

notes: Set 0 to disable. Counts added comments in all changed files; combines with narrating-comment and placeholder-comment content checks.

title: Dead interactive elements
summary: Every interactive element must have real behavior or be removed: a button or link that does nothing is a defect, not decoration; placeholders need a clear TODO in code and a visible label.

source.rule: R-26 — Interactive Elements
C-2 — Functional Completeness

tests.label: no-op button fails
tests.input: <button onClick={() => {}}>Upgrade</button>  // no handler body, no TODO + visible label

tests.label: real handler passes
tests.input: <button onClick={() => startTrial()}>Upgrade</button>

notes: Hard Gate rule. Acceptable placeholder only with a clear `// TODO` comment in code AND a visible 'Coming soon' label.

title: No file/CSS patching via scripts
summary: Implementing or altering features by running an external script that rewrites source or CSS with string replacement is broken by design; build features directly in source.

source.rule: R-33 — No File/CSS Patching via Scripts

tests.label: css patch script fails
tests.input:
# patch.py: rewrites app.css with string replacement to inject styles
css = open("app.css").read().replace(".btn", ".btn.custom")

tests.label: source-level styling passes
tests.input: .btn.custom { border-radius: 8px; }  // written directly in the stylesheet

notes: Hard Gate rule. A feature added by a patch script (e.g. Python editing .css files) must be rewritten in source.

title: Verify before you deliver
summary: A design or feature that has never been run or built is not finished: build it, check the console for errors, exercise every interactive element, and check themes and breakpoints before delivery.

source.rule: R-35 — Verify Before You Deliver

tests.label: delivered without running fails
tests.input: // PR shipped without running the app, no console check, interactive elements unexercised

tests.label: verified delivery passes
tests.input: // app built and run, console clean, every interactive element exercised, all themes/breakpoints checked

notes: Hard Gate rule. Includes 'no unverified builds': never deliver code whose build/runtime behavior is unobserved.

title: Real content or honest placeholder in code/docs
summary: Every claim, feature, or value embedded in code and its documentation must come from real information or be an explicitly labeled placeholder — never fabricate realistic-looking content, stats, or assertions.

source.rule: R-38 — Real Content or Honest Placeholder
R-36 — No Fabricated Claims

tests.label: invented stat fails
tests.input: const uptime = "99.99% SLA";  // no real SLO exists anywhere in the project

tests.label: labeled placeholder passes
tests.input: const uptime = "[REAL DATA]";  // explicitly labeled placeholder until the SLO is measured

notes: Hard Gate rule. Placeholders are written as what they are (`[REAL DATA]`, 'Coming soon'), never disguised as final; an empty section is better than a fabricated one. Unverified performance/security/compliance claims in code comments are covered here.

title: Wildcard imports
summary: `from module import *` (or `import *`) pulls every public name into the local namespace: dependencies become invisible, silent name collisions shadow real symbols, and static analysis and IDE navigation are defeated.

source.rule: Avoid wildcard imports (`from module import *`)
id: 'no-star-import' — description: 'from module import * pollutes the namespace and makes code harder to understand.'

tests.label: wildcard import fails
tests.input:
from os import *
from mypackage.helpers import *  # what shadows what?

tests.label: explicit names pass
tests.input:
from os.path import join
from mypackage.helpers import normalize, slugify

notes: Purpose-gate: a curated `__init__.py` re-export guarded by an explicit `__all__` is the accepted exception; prefer explicit re-exports even there.

title: Bare except with no exception type
summary: A bare `except:` (or `except BaseException:`) swallows everything, including KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit, making the program hard to interrupt and hiding real bugs; catch the narrowest type you can actually handle.

source.rule: Avoid bare / overly broad `except`

tests.label: bare except fails
narrow handler passes

notes: Complements ZS-CODE-023 (broad except that swallows with pass/None). A generic `except Exception` is tolerable only as a last-position handler that logs or re-raises; a bare `except:` is never.

title: Singleton comparison with `==` / identity check on values
summary: PEP 8 requires comparing None/True/False with `is`/`is not`, not `==`/`!=`: identity comparison is unambiguous and immune to objects overriding `__eq__`. Conversely, `is "literal"` tests object identity on values and silently breaks once interning stops.

source.rule: Compare singletons with `is`, not `==` (PEP 8)

tests.label: equality on singleton fails
identity on singletons passes

notes: `is`/`is not` is correct only for singletons; value comparison must use `==`/`!=`. Both directions of the confusion are the tell.

title: Magic numbers in business logic
summary: Unexplained numeric literals in comparisons and arithmetic force readers to reverse-engineer intent and make changes error-prone; non-obvious values belong in named, documented constants.

source.rule: Magic numbers — name your constants

tests.label: bare literals in logic fail
named constants pass
tests.input:
if retries > MAX_RETRIES:
    raise RetryExhausted
time.sleep(attempt * BASE_BACKOFF_SECONDS)
index += 1

notes: Heuristic: 0, 1, and -1 in conventional roles (indexing, increments, sentinels) are excluded; decimals in arithmetic are flagged. Triage non-obvious literals that should be constants.

title: Inline lint suppressions without justification
summary: `eslint-disable`, `# noqa`, and `# pragma: no cover` inserted to silence a linter instead of fixing the code are a classic AI-slop gaming move; each suppression should carry the reason it is genuinely required.

source.rule: Config Protection (Defense Against Rule-Gaming)

tests.label: blanket suppression fails
no suppressions passes
tests.input:
const legacy = payload;
x = foo()

notes: Triage: a suppression with an explicit reason (`// eslint-disable-next-line ... -- legacy types; see #88`) is acceptable; bare suppressions with no explanation are the tell.

title: Linter rule disabled in config
summary: Turning a lint rule `"off"`/`"ignore"` in .eslintrc, biome.json, .ruff.toml, or pyproject.toml to make violations pass instead of fixing code is rule-gaming; config changes that suppress violations need explicit review before merge.

source.rule: Config Tamper Guard

tests.label: rule set to off fails
rule kept on passes

notes: Matches rule ids (no-* names, Ruff/pylint/flake8/bandit codes) set to off/ignore in config files. Changing a rule to off to silence new violations is the slop signal; deliberate team-wide relaxations are triage-exempt.

title: Generic or empty error messages
summary: Error messages like 'Something went wrong', 'An error occurred', or an empty string carry no diagnosis; titles must be specific and searchable, naming what failed and why (never a bare 'Error').

matcher.pattern: (?:throw\s+new\s+\w*Error|raise\s+\w*Error|return\s+\w*Error)\(\s*["']\s*["']\s*\)|(?:throw\s+new\s+\w*Error|raise\s+\w*Error)\(\s*["'](?:something went wrong|an error occurred|unknown error|error occurred|internal error|unexpected error|oops!?|failed|error)[^"']*["']\s*\)(?!\s*[+%.,])

source.rule: Error message quality is a legitimate review item

tests.label: generic message fails
tests.input:
throw new Error("Something went wrong");
raise ValueError("Error")

tests.label: specific message passes
tests.input:
throw new Error(`Order ${id} failed: qty changed from ${before} to ${after}`);
raise ValueError(f"payment {code} declined")

notes: Static generic phrases only; messages that interpolate values (template literals, f-strings, concatenation) are exempt here and reviewed under ZS-CODE-047 for change context.

title: Custom exception class not derived from Exception
summary: A class named *Error/*Exception that does not inherit from the exception hierarchy cannot be raised or caught — `class PaymentError(object):` fails at runtime and breaks every except clause expecting it.

source.rule: Custom exceptions must derive from the exception hierarchy

tests.label: non-exception base fails
proper hierarchy passes

notes: Heuristic: names ending in Error/Exception are expected to derive from Exception (Python) or extend Error (TS). Subclasses of specific exceptions (ValueError, OSError) and *Error enums are accepted; object/BaseException bases are flagged. A class that is never raised is triage-exempt.

title: File crosses 1000-line boundary
summary: Pushing a file past ~1000 lines is a strong maintainability smell by default: the change should decompose into helpers, subcomponents, or modules first rather than letting the file sprawl.

source.rule: Do not let a PR push a file from under 1k lines to over 1k lines
Watch file size, not just diff size (~1000 total lines is a common inspection signal)
Watch file size, not just diff size. ... around 1000 *total* lines in a single file ... is a common inspection signal, not a hard cap. Decompose, then add.

tests.label: 1001-line file fails
380-line file passes

notes: Waivable only with a compelling structural reason and a clearly organized file; watch total file size in addition to diff size.

title: Destructive DB call with empty/None filter
summary: `frappe.db.set_value("Site", None, ...)` or `frappe.db.delete("Site")` with no filter updates or deletes every row in the table; these must error, never silently operate on the whole table.

source.rule: Watch for destructive DB APIs with empty/None filters

tests.label: filterless delete fails
tests.input:
frappe.db.delete("Site")           # deletes every row
doc = frappe.db.set_value("Site", None, "status", "Active")

tests.label: scoped filter passes
tests.input:
frappe.db.delete("Site", {"name": site_name})
frappe.db.set_value("Site", site_name, "status", "Active")

notes: The dangerous form is a quoted table/doctype name with no second argument (delete) or an explicit None/empty-string name (set_value/get_value). `from frappe import db` aliases are not caught by the regex — triage those.

title: Error message without change context
summary: An error thrown from a static literal cannot tell the user what changed; messages must reference the row, the field, and before→after values (e.g. 'qty changed from 1 → 2').

source.rule: State what changed: the row, the field, and before→after values

tests.label: static message fails
tests.input: throw new Error("Order qty changed");

tests.label: before/after values pass
tests.input:
throw new Error("Order " + id + " qty changed from " + before + " to " + after);
raise ValueError(f"qty {before} -> {after}")

notes: A message with no interpolation markers cannot carry the before→after context the reviewer needs. Generic phrases are also covered by ZS-CODE-043; this rule catches static messages regardless of wording.

title: God class over 500 lines
summary: A single class spanning more than 500 lines accumulates multiple responsibilities and forces readers to hold a huge state in mind; decompose it once the SRP boundary is crossed.

source.rule: No god classes (> 500 lines)

tests.label: 540-line class fails
120-line class passes

notes: Requires class-boundary extraction (AST); verify with wc -l-style counting of the class body. Complements the 1000-line file gate (ZS-CODE-045) at class granularity.

title: Untracked TODO/FIXME without ticket reference
summary: A `// TODO`/`FIXME` that names no ticket or issue is an untracked hack: per Broken Window theory it stays forever or is silently boarded up; every deferred item needs a tracked reference or a fix.

source.rule: Broken Window Theory: fix hacks immediately or board them up with a tracked ticket — never an untracked `// TODO`

id: 'no-ai-todo' — description: 'AI assistants leave placeholder TODOs that never get implemented.' — pattern targets (?:TODO|FIXME|HACK|XXX)\s*:?\s*(?:implement|add|fix|handle|replace|update|complete|finish|create|write|build|setup|configure|refactor)

tests.label: ticketless todo fails
tests.input:
// TODO: add retry here
# FIXME: handle pagination

tests.label: tracked todo passes
tests.input:
// TODO(#1234): add retry here
# FIXME: JIRA-42 handle pagination

notes: A reference immediately after the marker (ticket id, issue number, or bare 3+ digit id) counts as tracked. Multi-item numbered TODO lists without a ticket are flagged.

title: Generic except before specific handler
summary: Ordering `except Exception` before a more specific handler makes the specific clause dead code — it can never run; specific handlers must come first, with a generic `except Exception` only in last position.

source.rule: Prefer specific exception handlers — order handlers narrowest-first

tests.label: generic first fails
specific first passes

notes: Partial regex: matches an `except Exception` clause at the same indentation followed by a more specific `except X` in the same block. Tuple-form handlers (`except (A, B):`) and nested same-indent blocks are triage cases.

title: SQL built by string interpolation or concatenation
summary: Building SQL with f-strings or `"..." + var` invites injection and defeats parameterization; use the ORM/query builder or parameter substitution (`%s`, `?`, `:name`) exclusively.

source.rule: NEVER build SQL by string concatenation/f-strings
Are SQL queries parameterized (no string concatenation)?

tests.label: interpolated SQL fails
tests.input:
query = f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = {user_id}"
sql = "SELECT * FROM t WHERE x = " + x

tests.label: parameterized query passes
tests.input:
frappe.db.sql("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = %s", (user_id,))
rows = db.query("SELECT id FROM users WHERE id = ?", [uid])

notes: The tell is an f-prefixed SQL string or a quoted SQL literal concatenated with `+`; parameterized queries with placeholders pass. ORM builders (frappe.qb, query builders) are the preferred form.

title: Module mocking in tests (`vi.mock` / `jest.mock`)
summary: Vitest/Jest module mocking replaces a real dependency seam with a registry hack the test mutates, so the test passes against a mock and the module graph the app actually runs is never exercised.

source.rule: rejects Vitest and Jest `mock`, `doMock`, and `unstable_mockModule` calls in favor of real dependency seams.
Disallow Vitest and Jest module mocking; tests must replace dependencies through real interfaces.

tests.label: vi.mock call fails
typed spy on a real seam passes

notes: `vi.mocked(...)` (the typing helper) is deliberately not matched — only the registry-level `mock`/`doMock`/`unstable_mockModule` calls. Prefer injecting the collaborator (an interface the test implements) over module-level replacement.

title: Chained type assertions (`x as A as B`)
summary: Stapling two `as` clauses together fabricates evidence the compiler never checked — the middle type is an invented waypoint that makes the cast look reviewed. A single assertion documents one claim; a chain documents none.

source.rule: rejects nested `as` and angle-bracket assertions that fabricate evidence; chains made only of `as const` remain valid.
Disallow chained TypeScript as and angle-bracket assertions, including parenthesized chains.

tests.label: double as fails
tests.input:
const payload = JSON.parse(raw) as object as ParsedInvoice;
process(payload);

tests.label: single assertion and as const pass
tests.input:
const routes = ["/", "/pricing"] as const;
const config = loadConfig() as AppConfig;

notes: `as unknown as T` and `as any as T` are excluded on purpose: they are already the canonical `as any`/double-cast tell (ZS-CODE-008), so a chain there is not double-reported. Both type operands must be type-shaped (capitalized name, generic, or a primitive keyword) so English prose in comments ('as long as the run') cannot match. Parse at the boundary instead (`Schema.parse(raw)`).

title: Conditional empty-object spread to omit a field
summary: Spreading `{}` to drop a field makes the object's shape vary by an invisible branch; every consumer must model an optional key that is never written. Build the two shapes explicitly or assign `undefined` where the type says so.

source.rule: reports object spreads that use a conditional `{}` branch to omit fields. It intentionally has no autofix because omission is not equivalent to assigning `undefined`.
Disallow object spreads that conditionally spread an empty object to omit fields.

tests.label: empty else-branch spread fails
two concrete object branches pass

notes: The parenthesized spread is the only legal form of a spread ternary, so the pattern requires `...(` and a `{}` branch. Conditions containing their own parentheses are not inspected (miss, never a false hit).

title: Open dictionary value type (`Record<string, unknown|any|object>`)
summary: A dictionary whose direct value type is `unknown`, `any`, `object`, or `{}` is a property bag with no contract: every read needs a cast and every write is unchecked. Name the value type or keep the inferred shape.

source.rule: rejects dictionary value contracts based on `unknown`, `any`, `object`, `{}`, and semantic equivalents. Generic constraints such as `T extends Record<string, unknown>` are allowed.
Disallow object-dictionary contracts whose direct value type is unknown, any, object, {}.

tests.label: any-valued dictionary fails
generic constraint and named value type pass

notes: Only the direct value type is scanned: `Record<string, Item[]>` and `Record<string, Handler>` are fine. The `T extends Record<string, unknown>` generic-constraint form is exempted by lookbehind, per the upstream allowance.

title: Adjacent `filter()`/`map()` passes over the same array
summary: `filter().map()` (or `map().filter()`) walks the collection twice and allocates an intermediate array. Use `flatMap` for the transform-and-drop case or a lazy iterator pipeline.

source.rule: rejects adjacent eager array filter/map passes while allowing lazy iterator pipelines.
Chaining `.map().filter(Boolean)` creates an intermediate array and iterates twice. Use `.flatMap()` to transform and filter in a single pass.

tests.label: filter then map fails
tests.input: const emails = users.filter((user) => user.active).map((user) => user.email);

tests.label: single-pass flatMap passes
tests.input: const emails = users.flatMap((user) => (user.active ? [user.email] : []));

notes: Text-level rule: the two passes must be adjacent members of one chain (whitespace/newlines allowed, any other statement breaks the chain). A deliberate lazy iterator pipeline (`iter.values().filter(...).map(...)`) looks identical in source and is a known false positive — the upstream rule exempts it via type evidence the scanner does not have.

title: Missing blank line between top-level statements
summary: Structural blank lines are the cheapest map of a file: one group per declaration, one per logical block. Running a statement straight into the previous one (after a block, or after a lone `const`) erases those boundaries and reads as accreted edits.

source.rule: autofixes missing blank lines between top-level declarations, around multiline bindings, before control flow/returns, and after blocks; preserves compact groups of single-line bindings, imports, and overload signatures.
Require readable spacing between declarations and logical statement groups.

tests.label: import group not separated from first statement fails
binding followed by control flow fails
statement before control flow fails
spaced file with compact binding groups passes

notes: Executable slice of `require-readable-spacing` (an AST autofix rule upstream; four of its required-blank-line pairs are textually decidable at column 0): a `}`/`};` or single-line import followed by a statement, a single-line `const/let/var/using` followed by anything that is not another single-line binding, a single-line binding followed by an attached comment (the comment starts a new group; a trailing comment on the same line does not), and a statement followed by control flow. Checked against the upstream rule's own test corpus: 0 false positives on all 19 valid snippets and 11/15 invalid snippets caught; the misses are two statements sharing one line, a single-line block or declaration as the previous line (`if (ok) { go(); }`, `export interface A {}`), a previous line with no trailing `;`, and indented non-top-level code (the scanner's top-level proxy is column 0). Multi-line bindings after a binding and `function` overload groups also require the upstream AST rule.

title: Redundant boolean return (`if (c) { return true; } return false;`)
summary: Wrapping a boolean expression in an `if`/`return` pair before returning a literal adds a branch that carries no information — the predicate is already the answer.

source.rule: // SIMPLIFY: Redundant boolean return ... function isValid(input: string): boolean { if (input.length > 0 && input.length < 100) { return true; } return false; } // After: return input.length > 0 && input.length < 100;

tests.label: if/return-true then return-false fails
direct predicate return passes

notes: The `if` body must contain nothing but the literal return, immediately followed by the opposite literal return. Guard clauses that return a value or call a function in between are untouched.

title: Dead-code markers left in comments
summary: `// removed`, `// unused`, `// dead code`, `// might be useful later` and friends are tombstones: they keep the reader paying for code and intent that no longer exists. Delete the code — version control already remembers it.

matcher.pattern: ^[ \t]*(?:\*[ \t]*|//+[ \t]*|#+[ \t]*)(?:dead code\b|no longer used\b|not used(?: anymore)?\b|unused\b|removed\b|might (?:still )?be (?:useful|needed)(?: again)? later\b|kept for backwards? compat\w*|legacy shim\b)

source.rule: Are there dead code artifacts: no-op variables (`_unused`), backwards-compat shims, or `// removed` comments?
Dead code | Unreachable branches, unused variables, commented-out blocks | Remove (after confirming it's truly dead)

tests.label: removed/no-longer-used comment fails
intent comment passes

notes: Only line-leading comment markers count (a `//` inside a URL or a string cannot fire). The `_unused`-style no-op variable named in the same upstream checklist item needs scope evidence and is not covered here. Distinct from ZS-CODE-009/021 (placeholders for future work): these markers attest that code was deleted.

title: Await inside a loop body (sequential round trips)
summary: Awaited work executed one item at a time inside a loop turns N independent operations into N serialized round trips — the N+1 pattern. Batch them (`Promise.all`, a bulk API) or hoist the await out of the loop.

source.rule: No N+1 query patterns (use eager loading / joins) ... Bulk operations instead of loops of individual calls
When async operations have no interdependencies, execute them concurrently using `Promise.all()`. Incorrect (sequential execution, 3 round trips)

tests.label: await per item fails
batched await passes

notes: The window may not cross a closing brace, so awaits after the loop are never matched (no false hit from the statement that follows a loop); up to three `;`-separated statements inside the body are searched. `for await (... of stream)` iteration is not matched.

title: JSX `&&` rendering of a value that can be falsy (0/NaN)
summary: `{count && <Badge />}` renders the literal `0` (or `NaN`) instead of nothing, so zero-count rows gain a stray character. Guard with a comparison and render the fallback explicitly.

source.rule: Use explicit ternary operators (`? :`) instead of `&&` for conditional rendering when the condition can be `0`, `NaN`, or other falsy values that render. Incorrect (renders "0" when count is 0): {count && {count}}

tests.label: numeric && render fails
explicit ternary passes

notes: Scoped to numeric-shaped operands (`count`, `total`, `index`, `n...`, `.length`, `.size`) because those are the values that render as `0`; a boolean guard with a comparison (`items.length > 0 && (`) is already safe and is not matched.

title: Eager `useState(call())` initializer
summary: An initializer expression that is a function call (or `new ...`) runs on every render and is thrown away all but once. Pass a thunk (`useState(() => parseSettings())`) so the work happens on mount only.

source.rule: Pass a function to `useState` for expensive initial values. Without the function form, the initializer runs on every render even though the value is only used once. Incorrect (runs on every render): const [searchIndex, setSearchIndex] = useState(buildSearchIndex(items));

tests.label: useState(JSON.parse(...)) fails
lazy initializer passes

notes: Direct references, literals and primitives (`useState(0)`, `useState(props.initial)`, `useState(fn)`) do not match; only a call/new expression as the initializer does. `useState<T>(...)` with an explicit generic is out of scope (miss).

title: Untyped `any` annotations (`: any`, `<any>`)
summary: `any` in a type annotation silently disables checking for that value; the caller of the typed surface gets no guarantees. Replace with a specific type or `unknown` plus narrowing.

source.rule: id: 'any_type_usage' — pattern: /:\s*any\b/g — message: "Found 'any' type usage. Replace with specific type or unknown."
pattern: /:\s*any\b|as\s+any\b|<any\s*>/, messageTemplate: 'TypeScript `any` type bypasses type safety. Use a specific type.'

tests.label: any-annotated return fails
unknown-annotated return passes

notes: Scope narrowed per upstream: `as any` / `as unknown as T` are ZS-CODE-008; this rule covers annotations and type arguments (`Array<any>` is caught by the `<any>` branch). `unknown` is a compatible fix, not a violation.

title: Hallucinated React/Next imports from `react`
summary: `useRouter`, `Link`, `getServerSideProps` etc. do not exist in the `react` package; they come from `next/navigation`, `next/link`, or `next`. An import like this never resolves.

source.rule: id: 'hallucinated_react_import' — pattern: /import\s*{\s*(useRouter|useParams|useSearchParams|Link|Image|Script)\s*}\s*from\s*['"]react['"]/gi — message: "Hallucinated React import — these do NOT exist in 'react'"

id: 'hallucinated_next_import' — pattern: /import\s*{\s*(getServerSideProps|getStaticProps|getStaticPaths)\s*}\s*from\s*['"]react['"]/gi — message: "Next.js API imported from 'react' — 100% AI hallucination"

tests.label: useRouter from react fails
useRouter from next/navigation passes

notes: Upstream severity critical; a nonexistent specifier can never be deliberate. Verify the real import before using: hooks/router from next/navigation, Link from next/link, Image from next/image.

title: Imports of confirmed-nonexistent (hallucinated) packages
summary: AI models invent plausible package names that 404 on the registry; the import looks right in review but nothing resolves. This list was verified as nonexistent on npm/PyPI upstream.

source.rule: Confirmed nonexistent packages that AI models frequently hallucinate. Every entry verified as 404 on npm/PyPI as of April 2026. (jsPackages + pyPackages lists)
id: 'no-hallucinated-import-js' — description: "Detects imports of packages that are known AI hallucinations and don't exist on npm."

tests.label: hallucinated @langchain/agents import fails
tests.input:
import { AgentExecutor } from '@langchain/agents';

export const executor = new AgentExecutor({ verbose: true });

tests.label: real langchain subpath passes
tests.input:
import { AgentExecutor } from 'langchain/agents';

export const executor = new AgentExecutor({ verbose: true });

notes: Upstream notes the real package for each entry (e.g. '@anthropic/sdk' -> @anthropic-ai/sdk, 'pandas-profiler' -> ydata-profiling). Registry lists drift; re-verify an entry before removing it from the pattern.

title: Hedging comments in code
summary: Comments that say the code 'should work', is 'hopefully' correct or 'might not be the best approach' ship the author's uncertainty instead of knowledge; either fix the uncertainty or delete the comment.

source.rule: id: 'no-hedging-comments' — description: 'AI writes uncertain comments like "should work" or "might not be the best approach".'

id: 'hedging_uncertainty_comment' — pattern: /\/\/.*\b(should work|hopefully|probably|might work|try this|i think|seems to|attempting to|looks like|appears to)\b/gi — message: "AI hedging its bets — classic sign of low-confidence generation"

tests.label: hedged comment fails
factual comment passes

notes: Both upstream engines phrase this as an info-tier tell. Python `#` comments are covered by the same pattern (upstream ships a separate no-py-hedging-comments twin).

title: Overconfident comments
summary: Comments asserting that the code is 'obviously', 'clearly' or 'basically' correct pretend certainty the author never verified; upstream calls it the style/taste axis of AI slop.

source.rule: id: 'overconfident_comment' — pattern: /\/\/.*\b(obviously|clearly|simply|just|easy|trivial|basically|literally|of course|naturally|certainly|surely)\b/gi — message: "Overconfident comment — AI pretending it understands when it doesn't"

tests.label: overconfident comment fails
tests.input:
// obviously the connection pool is already warm here
const pool = getPool();

tests.label: specific comment passes
tests.input:
// The connection pool is primed by the prefetch worker before this runs.
const pool = getPool();

notes: Scope narrowed on purpose: upstream also fires on just/simply/easy/naturally, which false-positive on legitimate comments ('simply call the helper'); the retained set is the unambiguous certainty-asserting vocabulary.

title: Unverified-assumption comments
summary: Comments that record a guess — 'assuming the API returns a stable id', 'presumably this path is never taken' — leave reasoning nobody checked; dangerous when the assumption later changes.

source.rule: id: 'assumption_comment' — pattern: /\b(assuming|assumes?|presumably|apparently|it seems|seems like)\b.{0,50}\b(that|this|the|it)\b/gi — message: "AI making unverified assumptions — dangerous in production"

tests.label: assumption comment fails
tests.input:
// assuming the audit table exists on every tenant schema
const rows = await auditRepo.list(tenantId);

tests.label: verified statement passes
tests.input:
// The audit table exists on every tenant schema (created by migration 0042).
const rows = await auditRepo.list(tenantId);

notes: Comment-scoped (upstream matches prose anywhere, which catches identifiers like `assumedName`). Replace the guess with the verified fact or the check that proves it.

title: Numbered step comments
summary: '// Step 1: initialize the pool' style scaffolding comments narrate a procedure with a list marker; the code already sequences the steps. AI generates these constantly.

source.rule: id: 'no-step-comments' — description: 'AI generates numbered step comments like "Step 1: Initialize" that add noise.'

tests.label: step comment fails
tests.input:
// Step 1: initialize the connection pool
const pool = createPool(config);

tests.label: descriptive comment passes
tests.input:
// Create the pool once and share it across requests.
const pool = createPool(config);

notes: Covers `//` and Python `#` prefixes (upstream ships both). A real ordered procedure belongs in a docstring or README, not in per-line markers.

title: Nested ternary chains
summary: A ternary inside a ternary branch (`active ? 'On' : disabled ? 'Off' : 'Auto'`) is the classic 'looks clever' one-liner; a switch, lookup map or early returns read better.

source.rule: id: 'vibe_coded_ternary_abuse' — pattern: /\?\s*['"][^'"]+['"]\s*:\s*['"][^'"]+['"]\s*\?\s*['"][^'"]+['"]\s*:\s*['"][^'"]+['"]/g — message: "Nested ternary hell — AI trying to look clever"

tests.label: chained ternary fails
tests.input: const label = active ? "On" : disabled ? "Off" : "Auto";

tests.label: single ternary passes
tests.input: const label = active ? "On" : "Off";

notes: Generalized from the upstream string-literal form to any two chained ternaries on one line (bounded to a single line, optional chaining `?.` does not match). One nested ternary is a smell; a cluster is a confession.

title: AI attribution comments
summary: Comments that record model provenance ('Generated by ChatGPT', 'Generated with Claude Code', 'co-authored-by: claude') leak tooling into the repository and often violate internal policy; upstream ships them as auto-fixable.

source.rule: id: 'no-ai-attribution' — description: 'AI attribution comments leak model provenance into repos and often violate internal policies.' — severity: 'warn' — fix: 'remove-line'

tests.label: generated-by comment fails
tool-generated comment passes

notes: Wrapper/banner characters before the phrase are allowed (e.g. '// 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code]'). A generator script that is not a model ('Generated by scripts/gen-x.ts') is out of scope.

title: Mutable default arguments (Python)
summary: `def f(items=[])` / `= {}` / `= set()` shares one mutable object across calls — a classic gotcha AI generates; use `None` and assign inside the body.

source.rule: id: 'no-mutable-default' — description: 'Mutable default arguments (list, dict, set) are shared across calls. Classic Python gotcha AI generates.' — pattern: /def\s+\w+\s*\([^)]*(?:=\s*\[\s*\]|=\s*\{\s*\}|=\s*set\s*\(\s*\))/

tests.label: mutable defaults fail
None sentinel passes

notes: Upstream also excludes pydantic `Field(...)` defaults; that exemption is a repo-level call (allowlist if the codebase is declarative-model heavy).

title: Blanket `# type: ignore` without an error code
summary: A bare `# type: ignore` silences every diagnostic on the line, not just the intended one; upstream flags it as an AI tell because models use it to quiet mypy wholesale.

source.rule: id: 'no-type-ignore-blanket' — description: 'Blanket # type: ignore suppresses all type errors. AI uses this to silence mypy.' — pattern: /#\s*type:\s*ignore\s*$/ with antiPattern /#\s*type:\s*ignore\s*\[/

tests.label: blanket ignore fails
tests.input:
result = client.fetch(url)  # type: ignore
return result

tests.label: coded ignore passes
tests.input:
result = client.fetch(url)  # type: ignore[attr-defined]
return result

notes: Upstream's line-end anchor is replaced by a `\b` + lookahead so trailing commentary after the ignore is still caught while `type: ignore[...]` stays clean. Same family as ZS-CODE-008/ZS-CODE-041 for JS/Python lints.

title: RAW_SCROLL_LISTENER: raw scroll listener in script
summary: auteur's slopscan fails any script that reads scroll position through addEventListener('scroll') or an onscroll= attribute; the maintained replacement is IntersectionObserver or a CSS animation-timeline.

source.rule: const re = /addEventListener\s*\(\s*['"]scroll['"]/g; ... const re2 = /\bonscroll\s*=/g; findings.push({ rule: 'RAW_SCROLL_LISTENER', severity: 'fail', ... detail: `onscroll= attribute — use IntersectionObserver or animation-timeline` })

tests.label: fail - scroll listener
tests.input: window.addEventListener('scroll', onScroll);

tests.label: fail - onScroll JSX attribute
tests.input: <div onScroll={handleScroll} className="pane" />

tests.label: pass - intersection observer
tests.input:
const observer = new IntersectionObserver(onEnter);
observer.observe(sentinel);

notes: Purpose-gate (warning): a scroll listener that measures one element is a legitimate choice; the tell is scroll-driven layout or animation that the browser cannot optimize. Also the ui-domain form for markup (ZS-UI-121) stays in the ui engine.
